hero.heading: How much of your team's week goes to work your systems should be doing?
hero.subtitle: I guide you in building decisions into your systems: the ones already made and sitting in your wikis and meeting notes, and the ones that still need to be made. From then on, they get enforced without anyone watching or maintaining them.
hero.mode: The knowledge stays with your team: I design the approach we agree on, lead the implementation, and help where necessary.
hero.fit: For CIOs, CTOs, and engineering leaders whose system landscape has outgrown its structure.
whycurfee.heading.2: Anything a machine can check, a human should never have to check.
whycurfee.body.1: Every pragmatic decision adds another rule that the people in your organisation are asked to remember and check by hand.
whycurfee.body.2: I want organisations to invest their time and money in work that creates value for their business and employees. That's why I founded Curfee. I start:
whycurfee.start.1: With your system landscape that has grown organically.
whycurfee.start.2: With workflows that function because someone quietly maintains them.
whycurfee.start.3: With the decisions that have been made but never embedded.
whycurfee.highlight: Doing less is harder than doing more.
howiwork.1.title: Root cause over symptoms.
howiwork.1.body: Symptoms reveal the direction. Root causes demand resolution. The work begins where the chain ends.
howiwork.2.title: Addition by subtraction.
howiwork.2.body: Most system landscapes suffer from bloat: too many tools, standards that run on discipline, and inflated workflows. What no longer exists needs no maintenance and raises no questions.
howiwork.3.title: Make impossible, visible, or leave to judgment.
howiwork.3.body: Some violations must be impossible: data integrity, access, or legal requirements. Others stay visible as failing checks you can override with a reason. The work lies in deciding which rule goes where.
howiwork.4.title: Solid foundation over workaround.
howiwork.4.body: Workarounds lead to a structure that no one chose. A solid foundation comes first. Everything that follows builds on it.
howiwork.5.title: Rules stay changeable.
howiwork.5.body: Every decision built into the system has an owner and a cheap change path.
method.origins.heading: Why this approach
method.origin.1.title: Roots in logistics.
method.origin.1.body: I started by coordinating workflows between goods, employees, and processes. When people with different approaches work together, structure matters more than discipline.
method.origin.2.title: Documented and ignored.
method.origin.2.body: In software engineering and architecture, I kept watching well-documented decisions get ignored in practice. Once a decision lives in the structure, the agreed way becomes the only way.
method.origin.3.title: Improvements that compound.
method.origin.3.body: An embedded decision keeps paying off, while a shortcut keeps costing. When structure comes first, improvements compound instead of complexity.
method.origin.4.title: Structure in the age of AI.
method.origin.4.body: An AI does not get tired and does not forget the agreed way. It does not remember it either: whatever is not built into the system stays invisible.
hero.visual.aria: Diagram: recurring tasks that run on discipline, reduced to what matters and embedded as decisions the structure takes over
pattern.heading.status_quo: Does any of this sound familiar?
pattern.1.title: Discipline Dependency
pattern.1.reality: Conventions and knowledge live in people's heads. They work as long as someone is watching or maintaining them.
pattern.2.title: Structural Fragility
pattern.2.reality: Dependencies have grown beyond what anyone fully understands.
pattern.3.title: Decisions Without Effect
pattern.3.reality: Decisions were agreed on and documented on paper or in wikis, but nowhere did they get enforced consistently.
pattern.5.title: Workarounds as the Norm
pattern.5.reality: What started as an exception is now a new norm.
pattern.6.title: Invisible Routine
pattern.6.reality: Recurring tasks blend into everyday work until nobody notices how much time they take.
pattern.7.title: AI-Assisted Collaboration
pattern.7.reality: AI-generated content reaches your system landscape faster than your current structure can integrate it.
schema.service.description: Curfee offers enterprise architecture consulting for grown IT landscapes, delivered as high-value, project-based engagements rather than hourly services. Each engagement starts from the current reality of a system landscape, uncovers the root causes behind recurring struggles, and embeds decisions in pipelines and tooling so the system itself keeps them in effect, independent of individual discipline. Available across Austria, Germany, and Switzerland (DACH region).
about.heading: I am Philipp Höllinger.
engagements.heading: Selected engagements
engagements.1.label: Justice system
engagements.1.title: Double-booking a courtroom became impossible.
engagements.1.body: A court booking system enabled the very errors it was meant to prevent: double-booked courtrooms, past-dated bookings, unchecked conflicts. I guided the rebuild and designed integrity into every layer, from validation rules to database constraints.
engagements.1.diagram.aria: Diagram: a courtroom calendar where a second hearing in an occupied slot is refused and a hearing in a free slot is booked
engagements.2.label: Event platform
engagements.2.title: A summer job became a single click.
engagements.2.body: For years, five students spent each summer reading organiser emails and typing every event into the system by hand. I designed the flow around self-service: organisers submit their own listings and an automated import loads them daily. All that remains is to check the content, adjust a detail where needed, and click publish.
engagements.2.diagram.aria: Diagram: organisers fill a self-service event form, entries import daily, one click publishes them
engagements.2.diagram.form.title: Submit your event
engagements.3.label: Public administration
engagements.3.title: Every publication became bilingual.
engagements.3.body: The EU Single Digital Gateway required administrative information to be structured, multilingual, and machine-readable, yet no system could produce it. I designed the publishing system around predefined fields and a required translation step: editors fill the fields in German, and nothing goes live until the English translation exists. Metadata and publication run on their own.
engagements.3.diagram.aria: Diagram: editors fill predefined fields in German, a page can only go public once the English translation exists
engagements.3.diagram.form.title: Predefined fields
engagements.1.mechanism: Validation rules and database constraints refuse conflicting bookings on their own.
engagements.2.mechanism: The typing disappeared into a self-service structure with an automated import.
engagements.3.mechanism: Every page passes predefined fields and a hard publishing gate before it goes live.
engagements.4.label: Software development
engagements.4.title: An architecture violation becomes a failing build.
engagements.4.body: The pipeline checks layer rules and dependency directions. A PR that violates the architecture concept cannot merge. Reviewers stop policing conventions and review what machines cannot judge: design intent and tradeoffs.
engagements.4.mechanism: A merge now requires passing architecture tests and CI gates.
engagements.4.diagram.aria: Diagram: a pull request check list where build and tests pass, the architecture check fails, and the merge is blocked
engagements.4.diagram.title: Pull request checks
engagement.heading: The engagement
engagement.math: Ten minutes, twice a day, across twenty people: that is a working month every year, spent on one check the system should do.
engagement.1.title: The Audit
engagement.1.outcome: You know where your team keeps the rules in its head, where it checks by hand, and where to start.
engagement.1.deliver.1: A written overview of the rules your team actually works by, the documented ones and the ones that only live in people's heads.
engagement.1.deliver.2: A decision for each of them: make it impossible to break, make it visible, or leave it to judgment.
engagement.1.deliver.3: A plan for which rules to build into the system first, and what each step depends on.
engagement.1.expect.1: The rules in one place, in the words your team already uses.
engagement.1.expect.2: A first step small enough to begin the week after.
engagement.1.expect.3: A straight answer on what is not worth doing at all.
engagement.1.how: I work through interviews with the people involved and trace past incidents back to their causes, alongside what is already documented. A conversation of 30 to 60 minutes per person is enough.
engagement.1.fact.1.label: Duration
engagement.1.fact.2.label: Scope
engagement.2.title: Guided Embedding
engagement.2.outcome: The rules that used to run on discipline now run in your systems.
engagement.2.deliver.1: Checks and rules we build into your systems.
engagement.2.deliver.2: A written schedule for what gets built in which month.
engagement.2.deliver.3: An owner and a cheap change path for every rule.
engagement.2.expect.1: Rules that keep working when the people who wrote them move on.
engagement.2.expect.2: Reviewers who stop policing conventions and judge design instead.
engagement.2.expect.3: A team that knows why each check exists.
engagement.2.how: I set the direction, shape the design with your team, and make sure each rule works the way it was meant to.
engagement.2.fact.1.label: Duration
engagement.2.fact.2.label: Scope
engagement.3.title: Staying on Track
engagement.3.outcome: When your organisation changes, the decisions stay in the structure, and it keeps fitting the way you work.
engagement.3.deliver.1: A regular written review: what changed, what still applies, what needs a decision.
engagement.3.deliver.2: New rules built in as they are decided.
engagement.3.deliver.3: Existing checks adjusted when tools, teams, and requirements change.
engagement.3.expect.1: A structure that still fits after a reorganisation or a change of tools.
engagement.3.expect.2: Rules retired once they stop earning their place.
engagement.3.expect.3: A record of why each rule exists, kept current.
engagement.3.how: I review what changed, adjust the rules with your team, and name what needs a decision.

about.who.quote: What drives me is an obsession with the things that go unnoticed, the small details that shape the future of an environment.
about.who.why.3: Before I change anything, I want to understand how it affects an organisation and the people working with it. The most common mistake I have seen is the opposite: systems and the workflows between them, implemented first and understood later.
about.who.why.2: I am a minimalist and call myself an advocate of simple concepts. They outlast any sophisticated process that runs on discipline and quietly breaks over time. And small changes that keep paying off over time create as much value as one big fix for one big pain.

privacy.personal: Personal data is collected only to the extent technically necessary, with purpose limitation and data minimisation applied throughout. Collected data is never disclosed to third parties without a legal basis. Three legal grounds may apply. Consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR) covers cases where you have given consent for one or more specific purposes. Performance of a contract (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR) covers cases where processing is needed to perform a contract you are party to, or to take steps at your request before entering into one. Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR) covers cases where processing is necessary for legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, unless those interests are overridden by your fundamental rights and freedoms.
privacy.rights.heading: Rights of data subjects
privacy.rights: As a data subject, you have the following rights. Access (Art. 15 GDPR): confirmation whether your personal data is being processed, along with information about such data and its processing. Rectification (Art. 16 GDPR): correction of inaccurate or incomplete personal data. Erasure (Art. 17 GDPR): deletion of your personal data, subject to the conditions laid down in Art. 17. Restriction of processing (Art. 18 GDPR): limits on how your personal data is processed. Data portability (Art. 20 GDPR): a copy of your personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format. Objection (Art. 21 GDPR): the right to object at any time, on grounds relating to your particular situation, to processing of your personal data.

faq.heading: Questions you might have.
faq.1.question: How is this different from classic enterprise architecture?
faq.1.answer: Classic enterprise architecture produces target pictures for slides and governance for boards. I start from the reality of your system landscape, and with your team we build decisions into your systems: the ones already made, and the ones still to be made.
faq.2.question: What does "decisions that enforce themselves" mean?
faq.2.answer: It means decisions are built into the system itself, and from then on the system applies them, independent of individual discipline. Some violations become impossible, others stay visible, and the rest is left to judgment. What lives in the system stays intact until change is necessary.
faq.3.question: How does an engagement with me work?
faq.3.answer: An engagement is a project scoped to one area of your organisation. I talk with your team, design the approach, and reduce the area to its essentials. Then we build the checks into your systems.
faq.4.question: Who do I work with?
faq.4.answer: Decision-makers whose system landscape has outgrown its structure, in Austria, Germany, and Switzerland, from mid-sized companies to single corporate units. The best fit is an organisation that wants the decisions it has made to take effect reliably. I work remotely in English or German.
faq.5.question: Do we need new tools for this?
faq.5.answer: Usually not. We embed the conventions, standards, and checks into the systems already in place.
faq.6.question: What happens when tools, teams, or requirements change?
faq.6.answer: Every rule built into the system has an owner and a cheap change path. Staying on Track covers this in a rhythm that fits your organisation.
faq.7.question: How much of your team's time does this take?
faq.7.answer: The audit takes 30 to 60 minutes per person. During the embedding we build the checks in the hours your team already spends on the system. Nobody is pulled onto a project on the side.
